name: Nano zinc oxide
lead: Nano zinc oxide refers to zinc oxide particles in the nanometre size range, used in sunscreens and other personal-care products as a mineral UV filter. Grokipedia states that the small size permits higher loadings without the white cast of larger particles, and that particles are often silica-coated to limit reactivity on skin [1].

The question researchers and regulators focus on is whether nanoparticles enter the body through skin. The same page reports negligible dermal penetration in human studies, with particles remaining in the stratum corneum, though some in vitro models suggest minor translocation under extreme conditions; the page carries a caveat about internal inconsistencies in its figures [1].

In the EU, cosmetic ingredients in nano form must be labelled "nano" under Regulation 1223/2009, and sunscreen use is assessed by the SCCS; US rules do not require nanoparticle labelling [1][2]. Laboratory studies document antibacterial activity and toxicity to aquatic organisms and cells in culture [3][4][5].

paras: Nano zinc oxide gives broad UVA and UVB protection, by reflecting and scattering light according to Grokipedia, with a sheerer finish than larger particles [1]. Wikipedia likewise notes that many sunscreens use nanoparticles because they do not scatter visible light and so look transparent [6]. Other personal-care uses include anti-dandruff products [1]. Research uses include wound dressings, textiles and dental materials [7][8].

Grokipedia reports negligible penetration in human studies and says the EU SCCS endorsed coated zinc oxide nanoparticles up to 25% for non-sunscreen dermal uses in 2016, conditional on low photoreactivity and particle size distribution under 100 nm [1]. A related wiki page notes that FDA classifies zinc oxide as GRASE for sunscreen without nano-specific restrictions [2].

Laboratory studies show cytotoxicity from reactive oxygen species and dissolved zinc, and iron doping has been explored to make the particles less toxic [4][5]. Marine organism studies report toxicity that depends on aggregate size and ion solubility [9]. Dissolution in different matrices has also been measured [10].

No studies found of nano zinc oxide for appearance outcomes. Registered trials using zinc oxide nanoparticles are dental, for example cavity disinfection (NCT03478150, n=30) [11]. Laboratory and animal work on antibacterial and wound-dressing uses is a separate category [3][7].

Nano versus non-nano mineral sunscreen is a recurring theme in skincare discussions: some users prefer non-nano labels out of caution about nanoparticles, while others prefer sheer nano formulas for lack of white cast. These are general sunscreen views rather than documented claims.

card.summary: Nanoparticle zinc oxide: the invisible-on-skin version of the mineral filter, with debate centred on penetration and aquatic toxicity.
card.note: EU requires a "nano" label; US does not.

quick.overview:
Nano zinc oxide is zinc oxide in nanometre-sized particles, used so mineral sunscreens look transparent instead of white.

Human studies summarised in reference works report particles staying in the outer skin layer. No studies of appearance outcomes were found.
quick.mechanism: It reflects, scatters and absorbs UVA and UVB light; particles are often coated, for example with silica, to limit reactivity.
quick.risks: Laboratory studies report cytotoxicity and aquatic toxicity linked to dissolved zinc and reactive oxygen species. The EU requires nano labelling; the US does not.
